sec-cryptography-symmetric-asymmetric-ha.core: Cryptography provides confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation. Use symmetric AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for data, asymmetric keys (X25519, Ed25519) for key exchange and signatures, modern hashes (SHA-256, BLAKE3) for fingerprints, and Argon2id with salts for passwords. Quantum computers threaten public-key crypto, so plan hybrid post-quantum migration (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) for long-lived data.

first_principles.problem: Misused crypto creates a false sense of security.

analogy.title: Envelopes, seals and fingerprints
analogy.story: Hide, prove origin, detect tampering.
analogy.breaks: Physical seals are forgeable.

check.q: Which algorithms should you use for data encryption and password storage respectively?
check.a: An AEAD cipher like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for data, and a slow salted password hash like Argon2id for passwords.

sec-identity-oidc-saml-rbac-abac.core: IAM separates authentication from authorisation. Federation via SAML (signed XML assertions) or OIDC (ID tokens, built on OAuth access tokens) centralises login, and Authorization Code with PKCE secures browser and mobile flows. RBAC maps job functions to roles, and ABAC adds attribute-based policies for context such as tenant and region. Automate lifecycle and review access regularly.

first_principles.problem: Scattered credentials and coarse access lead to breaches and slow offboarding.

analogy.title: Passports, visas and border rules
analogy.story: Prove identity once, get scoped permissions everywhere.
analogy.breaks: Passports last years; tokens should be short.

example.title: SaaS identity stack
flow: RBAC roles + Cedar ABAC for tenancy

check.q: Which OAuth/OIDC flow should a single-page app use?
check.a: Authorization Code with PKCE (ideally via a backend-for-frontend), not the deprecated implicit flow.

sec-modern-auth-fido2-webauthn-passkeys.core: Passwords and OTP codes are phishable shared secrets. FIDO2/WebAuthn replaces them with per-site key pairs that sign server challenges with origin binding, so lookalike sites get nothing. Passkeys make that usable through synced, biometric-unlocked credentials (with device-bound keys for high-risk roles), and device posture adds context so access depends on both who you are and what you're using.

first_principles.problem: Phishing and credential theft bypass passwords and weak MFA.

analogy.title: A key that fits only the real door, checked with your health pass
analogy.story: Fakes can't use it, and unsafe visitors don't get in.
analogy.breaks: Physical keys copy; passkeys are bound.

check.q: What property makes FIDO2 credentials phishing-resistant?
check.a: They are cryptographically scoped to the relying party's origin (RP ID), so a phishing domain can't obtain a valid signature.

sec-jwks-json-web-key-sets.core: Shared HMAC secrets let any verifier forge tokens, while asymmetric signing keeps the private key with the issuer and publishes public keys in a JWKS selected by kid via OIDC discovery. Rotate by pre-publishing, overlapping and removing after expiry; cache the JWKS with refetch on unknown kid (rate-limited); and defend against alg, jku and kid attacks by pinning algorithms, using a fixed JWKS URL and validating every claim.

first_principles.problem: Token verification is either insecure (shared secrets) or brittle (hardcoded keys).

analogy.title: A king's seal with a public specimen directory
analogy.story: Only the king seals; everyone checks against the official directory.
analogy.breaks: Specimens don't rotate quarterly.

example.title: API verification standard
flow: IdP signs ES256 with KMS key
JWKS at fixed URL, 10 min cache

check.q: What three checks besides the signature must every JWT verifier perform?
check.a: Validate the issuer (iss), audience (aud) and expiry (exp), with algorithms pinned to an allowed list.

sec-jit-access-ephemeral-privileges.core: Standing privileges are always exploitable. Just-in-time access replaces them with request, approve, grant and revoke flows (risk-tiered approvals, time-bound grants, full audit), implemented natively in each cloud (AWS Identity Center/TEAM, GCP PAM, Azure PIM) and made frictionless through Slack and CLI automation, with sealed, monitored break-glass accounts for when the system itself fails.

first_principles.problem: Permanent admin access turns any compromise into a major breach.

analogy.title: Signing out the master key
analogy.story: Borrow briefly, return automatically, emergency axe behind glass.
analogy.breaks: Keys need returning by hand.

example.title: Programme
flow: JIT via Slack with on-call auto-approve

check.q: What is 'zero standing privilege'?
check.a: A state where no user holds elevated permissions permanently; privileges are granted just in time and expire automatically.

sec-owasp-top-10-injection-xss-ssrf.core: The OWASP Top 10 groups the web's most common vulnerabilities into classes that share root causes: missing server-side authorization (A01), weak or absent crypto and insecure defaults (A02/A05), and untrusted input interpreted as code by SQL engines, browsers or URL fetchers (A03, A10). The defensive pattern repeats across them: deny by default, keep code and data separate, encode output for its context, validate destinations, and automate checks so regressions are caught.

first_principles.problem: A product team fixes bugs one at a time and keeps seeing new variants of the same few classes.

analogy.title: Building codes for houses
analogy.story: Fire, flood and break-ins are known hazards; codes specify fire doors and locks so each builder doesn't relearn them.
analogy.breaks: Building codes are law; OWASP is voluntary, so teams must choose to adopt it.

steps.label: A01
steps.detail: Check that the user owns the profile.

steps.label: A03
steps.detail: Encode the alt text on render.

check.q: What do injection, XSS and SSRF have in common?
check.a: Untrusted input is interpreted by a powerful component (a DB, browser or HTTP client) without separation or validation.

sec-api-security-bola-data-exposure-rate.core: APIs expose business logic directly to scripts, so their security must not depend on any client. Every request needs a valid, short-lived credential (authentication), a check that this caller may touch this specific object (BOLA), strict schemas that control exactly which fields come in and go out (data exposure, mass assignment, injection), and limits on volume (rate limiting). Together with an accurate inventory, these turn an open loading dock into a controlled gate.

first_principles.problem: A fintech's mobile API leaks other users' transactions, accepts role fields, and is credential-stuffed overnight.
truths: Each request must stand on its own checks.

analogy.title: An airport security pipeline
analogy.story: ID check, boarding-pass match, bag scan and queue control: each catches something the others miss.
analogy.breaks: Airports have one entrance; APIs have hundreds of endpoints, each needing every check.

check.q: Why is BOLA so common in APIs?
check.a: APIs expose object IDs in every request, and each handler must remember an ownership check.

sec-scanning-sast-dast-sca-container-run.core: Each scanner type sees software from a different angle. SAST reads your code, SCA reads your dependency list, container scanning reads your image, DAST attacks the running app, and runtime protection watches production behaviour. None is complete alone. A mature pipeline layers them from IDE to production, gates only on high-confidence and fixable findings, and feeds results into one triage queue so developers fix the right things first.

first_principles.problem: A team runs one scanner and is surprised by breaches through dependencies, misconfig and runtime exploits.

analogy.title: Layers of quality control in a car factory
analogy.story: Parts are checked on arrival, the assembly is tested, the finished car is crash-tested, and then telemetry watches it on the road.
analogy.breaks: Car recalls are rare; software CVEs arrive daily.

example.title: Pipeline map
example.outcome: defence in depth across the lifecycle.

check.q: Which scanner would catch a vulnerable transitive dependency?
check.a: SCA (or a container scanner reading the image's packages).

sec-threat-modeling-stride-attack-trees.core: Threat modeling turns security from reaction into design. You draw the system (DFD with trust boundaries), enumerate what can go wrong systematically (STRIDE per element, attack trees per attacker goal), rank by likelihood and impact so effort goes to the biggest risks, then validate assumptions with red and purple teams. It finds design flaws no scanner will, while they are still cheap to fix.

first_principles.problem: Breaches keep exploiting design assumptions such as trusted headers, missing MFA and flat networks that were never questioned.

analogy.title: An architect's structural review before building
analogy.story: Engineers calculate loads and failure modes on paper, then stress-test models, before pouring concrete.
analogy.breaks: Physics is fixed; adversaries adapt, so models need regular refreshing.

steps.label: Find
steps.detail: Plaintext SFTP creds in config (I, S).

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: Red team attempts exfiltration; detection fires.

check.q: How do STRIDE and attack trees differ in perspective?
check.a: STRIDE starts from system elements; attack trees start from the attacker's goal.

sec-social-engineering-phishing-physical.core: Social engineering attacks the human layer through psychological levers (authority, urgency, curiosity, helpfulness, reciprocity) across email, phone, SMS and physical access. Because people can't be patched and someone will always be fooled, defence focuses on making a single fooled person insufficient (phishing-resistant MFA, dual approval, device control, 802.1X), giving clear verification rules, and building a no-blame culture where fast reporting turns every employee into a sensor.

first_principles.problem: Despite heavy security spending, attackers keep getting in by calling, texting or walking in.
truths: Humans are targeted because it works.

analogy.title: A bank vault with a talkative clerk
analogy.story: The steel is impregnable, so robbers talk to the clerk instead. The fix is dual-key procedures, not just a stronger door.
analogy.breaks: Bank clerks are few; every employee in a company is a potential target.

example.title: A multi-channel attack

steps.label: Break 2
steps.detail: Callback rule exposes the fake IT call.

steps.label: Break 3
steps.detail: FIDO2 means there's no push to approve.

example.outcome: each layer can stop the chain.

check.q: What single control most reduces credential-phishing impact?
check.a: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys), because credentials entered on a fake site don't work.

sec-secrets-management-vault-aws-eso-hsm.core: Secrets management replaces scattered, long-lived credentials with a governed system. Secrets live centrally (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), encrypted under keys rooted in hardware (HSM/KMS). Workloads authenticate with identity they already have (Kubernetes, IAM, OIDC) rather than another secret. Credentials are ideally dynamic and short-lived, delivered into platforms like Kubernetes through references (ESO), and every access is audited.

first_principles.problem: An org has passwords in Git, shared DB users, no rotation and no idea who accessed what.
truths: Trust must bottom out in hardware.

analogy.title: A modern hotel key system
analogy.story: A central system (Vault) programs a key card per guest (dynamic secret) after checking ID (auth method), cards expire at checkout (TTL), and the master encoder is locked away (HSM).
analogy.breaks: Hotels have one building; secrets span clouds, clusters and CI.

example.title: Pod to database, no stored secret

check.q: What eliminates the need to rotate a DB password?
check.a: Dynamic secrets: each credential is short-lived and revoked automatically.

sec-advanced-key-management-byok-hyok-mp.core: Advanced key management is about deciding who can decrypt. Provider-managed keys are easy but give the provider control. Customer-managed keys add your policies. BYOK proves the key's origin and lets you revoke it. HYOK/XKS keeps the key outside the cloud so the provider must ask you every time. MPC eliminates any single whole key. Each step trades operational effort and availability risk for control, so you choose per data class.

first_principles.problem: Regulated, multi-cloud data needs demonstrable control over who can decrypt, without crippling availability.

analogy.title: Escalating levels of personal security
analogy.story: A doorman, your own lock, a safe only you can open, or a treasure that needs several trustees together.
analogy.breaks: Higher security means you carry the risk of lockout.

check.q: Which model lets you prove the provider cannot decrypt without you?
check.a: HYOK/XKS, where every decrypt calls your external key store.

sec-attestation-chains-tpm-secure-boot.core: Attestation chains build trust from hardware upward. An immutable root (boot ROM plus TPM) measures each stage before it runs, extending hashes into extend-only PCRs (Measured Boot), while Secure Boot refuses unsigned code. The TPM can seal secrets to those measurements and sign quotes so remote verifiers can confirm, with a fresh nonce, exactly what booted. IMA extends this into runtime. The result: secrets and access are released only to machines that can prove they're healthy.

first_principles.problem: Infrastructure must ensure only uncompromised machines get disk keys, credentials and network access.
truths: Proof must be fresh and hardware-signed.

analogy.title: A chain of custody for evidence
analogy.story: Each handler signs a log before passing the item on, starting from a trusted collector, so a court can verify nothing was swapped.
analogy.breaks: Paper logs can be forged; PCRs can't be rewritten.

check.q: What's the difference between sealing and attestation?
check.a: Sealing releases a local secret only in a given state; attestation proves that state to a remote party.

sec-confidential-computing-tees-sgx-nitr.core: Confidential computing protects data in use, the last unencrypted state. Hardware TEEs isolate code and encrypt its memory so even the host OS, hypervisor and cloud operator can't read it. They come as process enclaves (SGX, smallest TCB), confidential VMs (SEV-SNP, TDX, no app changes) or isolated enclaves (Nitro). Remote attestation proves genuine hardware and expected code, and secrets are released only to attested instances. It pays off where you can't trust the operator or must compute jointly across organisations.

first_principles.problem: Sensitive workloads need the cloud's scale without trusting its administrators with plaintext.

analogy.title: A sealed, inspected glovebox in someone else's lab
analogy.story: You use their facilities, but the samples stay sealed, and a certificate proves the box is genuine and unopened.
analogy.breaks: Side channels mean the glass isn't perfectly opaque.

example.title: Private inference
example.scenario: Encrypted prompt to a confidential GPU VM.

steps.label: Return
steps.detail: Only the client can read it.

check.q: Which TEE type requires the fewest application changes?
check.a: Confidential VMs (SEV-SNP or TDX), which run unmodified OSes and applications.

sec-zero-trust-mtls-spiffe-boundary.core: Zero trust replaces 'inside the network means trusted' with per-request verification of identity, context and policy. For machines, that means mTLS with unique, short-lived workload identities issued through platform attestation (SPIFFE/SPIRE), with no shared certs or pre-shared secrets. For humans, identity-aware proxies (Boundary, Teleport) replace VPNs with per-target, posture-checked, recorded sessions using brokered credentials. Network position stops being a credential.

first_principles.problem: A single phished VPN user or compromised pod can reach everything on a flat, trusted internal network.
truths: Identity must be strong and specific.
Access should be per request and per target.

analogy.title: An airport where every gate re-checks your boarding pass and passport
analogy.story: Passing security doesn't let you board any plane; each gate verifies you belong on that flight.
analogy.breaks: Airports have one flight per gate; services have many callers and need automated checks.

example.title: Human and machine paths
flow: Engineer: SSO+MFA → proxy → one DB (brokered creds)
Service: SPIRE SVID → mTLS → authz on SPIFFE ID

check.q: What replaces network location as the basis for access in zero trust?
check.a: Verified identity (user or workload) plus device and context, evaluated against policy per request.

sec-opa-gatekeeper-policy-enforcement.core: Kubernetes is open by default, and RBAC controls who can act, not what they create. OPA Gatekeeper adds policy-as-code at the admission webhook, the single choke point for all writes. Rules are written in Rego, packaged as reusable ConstraintTemplates, instantiated as parameterised Constraints, rolled out safely through dryrun → warn → deny with audit of existing resources, and complemented by mutations that apply secure defaults automatically.

first_principles.problem: Clusters accumulate privileged pods, untrusted images and unlabelled workloads despite written standards.
truths: All writes pass the API server.

analogy.title: Automated building codes with a site inspector at the only gate
analogy.story: Codes are written once, applied with local parameters, introduced with warnings, and some small fixes are made on the spot.
analogy.breaks: Real inspectors use judgement; policies do exactly what they're written to do.

check.q: Why does Gatekeeper mutation run before validation?
check.a: So objects can be made compliant first and then still be checked by validating constraints.

sec-ebpf-tetragon-falco.core: eBPF turns the Linux kernel into a safe, programmable sensor and enforcement point. Verified programs attach to hooks (tracepoints, kprobes, uprobes, LSM, XDP), seeing exactly what the kernel acts on and avoiding the TOCTOU races of user-space monitors. Falco uses this for rule-based detection with Kubernetes context; Tetragon adds synchronous in-kernel enforcement such as killing a process mid-syscall. With Cilium for networking, they give full runtime security for containers.

first_principles.problem: Containers are scanned and admitted correctly, yet runtime attacks go unseen and unstopped.

analogy.title: A building with sensors in the walls, cameras and guards
analogy.story: Sensors in the walls (eBPF) can't be bypassed, cameras (Falco) record and alert, and guards (Tetragon) intervene.
analogy.breaks: Building sensors are installed once; eBPF programs load and update dynamically.

example.title: Detect vs prevent
flow: Attacker runs curl | sh in pod
Tetragon: Sigkill on exec of /bin/sh in namespace web

check.q: What's the key difference between Falco and Tetragon?
check.a: Falco primarily detects and alerts; Tetragon can also enforce synchronously in the kernel.

sec-cspm-agentless-wiz-orca.core: In the cloud, the main exploit is misconfiguration, not zero-days. CSPM continuously inventories every account through provider APIs and checks configuration against benchmarks. Agentless platforms add deep workload visibility by snapshot sidescanning, giving full coverage in minutes with no installs, while agents or eBPF handle real-time blocking. A security graph connects exposure, vulnerabilities, identities and data to surface the few toxic attack paths worth fixing first, and the same data automates compliance evidence.

first_principles.problem: A multi-cloud estate has thousands of findings, partial agent coverage and painful audits.

analogy.title: A city map with every building, door and road, plus a planner who highlights only the routes a burglar could actually use
analogy.story: You fix those routes, not every crack in every pavement.
analogy.breaks: City maps change slowly; cloud estates change by the minute.

example.title: From findings to fix
flow: Graph: Internet → VM (CVE) → Role → PII bucket

check.q: Why combine agentless and agent-based approaches?
check.a: Agentless gives fast, complete posture coverage; agents/eBPF give real-time detection and blocking.

sec-data-lakes-telemetry-siem-hunting.core: Security operations depend on data. Collect the telemetry triad (endpoint, network, identity/cloud), route it through a pipeline that normalises (OCSF) and tiers it: high-value events to the SIEM for real-time detection, everything to a cheap, well-partitioned data lake for retention and hunting. Engineer detections as code (Sigma, Git, tests, ATT&CK mapping) and hunt proactively for what detections miss, turning each successful hunt into a new detection.

first_principles.problem: A SOC is drowning in cost and noise yet blind to stealthy attackers.

analogy.title: A city's surveillance system
analogy.story: Live monitors for key junctions (SIEM), recordings of everything archived (lake), alarm rules tested and versioned (detection as code), and detectives reviewing footage for patterns (hunting).
analogy.breaks: Cities watch streets; logs must be normalised across hundreds of formats.

check.q: Why send all logs to a data lake but only some to the SIEM?
check.a: The lake stores everything cheaply for hunting and retention, while the SIEM's costly real-time engine handles high-value detection data.

sec-compliance-architectures-fips-fedram.core: Compliance frameworks convert legal and market requirements into engineering constraints. FIPS dictates validated cryptographic modules, FedRAMP requires NIST 800-53 controls inside a tight authorisation boundary, GDPR makes geography and data subject rights architectural, and PCI DSS makes scope reduction through tokenisation the key strategy. Treated as continuous engineering (controls as code, continuous monitoring, automated evidence mapped to many frameworks), compliance becomes a property of the system rather than an annual scramble.

first_principles.problem: Each new market or customer brings a new framework, an audit fire drill and an architecture surprise.

analogy.title: Designing a building to meet fire, accessibility and health codes from the start
analogy.story: One good design satisfies several codes, and sensors prove it daily rather than once a year.
analogy.breaks: Building codes change rarely; regulations and cloud estates both change often.

steps.label: Scope
steps.detail: Keep regulated data in small zones.

check.q: Which single PCI strategy most reduces engineering burden?
check.a: Tokenisation with a certified provider, which keeps card data out of your systems.

sec-privacy-engineering-dp-kanonymity-to.core: Privacy engineering gives data utility while limiting risk to individuals. It starts with minimisation and real erasure (data maps, TTLs, crypto-shredding), applies tokenisation to keep sensitive values out of operational systems, and treats pseudonymised data as still personal. For sharing and publishing, it uses anonymisation techniques with known limits: k-anonymity hides who but not what and fails under linkage, while differential privacy provides mathematical guarantees through calibrated noise and a privacy budget.

first_principles.problem: An organisation must analyse and share customer data while meeting GDPR and avoiding re-identification scandals.

analogy.title: Layers of disguise matched to how public the setting is
analogy.story: At home you use your name; at work a badge number (token); in a published photo you're blurred into the crowd (k-anon); in census statistics you're a fuzzy contribution to a total (DP).
analogy.breaks: Disguises are visual; data re-identification uses joins and statistics.

check.q: Why is differential privacy considered stronger than k-anonymity?
check.a: It gives a mathematical guarantee that holds regardless of the attacker's auxiliary knowledge, which k-anonymity can't.
